title: Epictetus goes free
hook: freed, he teaches in Rome, is banished with all philosophers by Domitian, and opens a school at Nicopolis around 93 CE

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epictetus, and a man who answered calmly. Your line was said calmly. When something you couldn't change went wrong, what voice did you answer in? Day twenty-four.

We left Epictetus enslaved, with a leg that would never work properly again. Here's what happened next. At some point, and we don't know exactly when or how, he was set free. He'd already been studying philosophy while enslaved, with a Roman Stoic teacher named Musonius Rufus. Now he started teaching it himself, in Rome. A lame, formerly enslaved man, teaching the sons of the powerful how to live. And then the emperor Domitian decided philosophers were a nuisance and threw them all out of the city.
screen: `SET FREE, SOMEHOW.` → `A LAME MAN TEACHING IN ROME.` → `THE EMPEROR THROWS THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: Domitian expelled the philosophers from Rome; historians still debate the exact year. Epictetus lost his city, his students, whatever he'd built. So he went across the sea to Nicopolis, a town on the western coast of Greece, and opened a school. And people came. Young men traveled, some of them a long way, to sit on hard benches and be questioned by this lame teacher. As far as we know, Epictetus never wrote a book. We have his teaching only because one student, Arrian, wrote down what he said, and later published it as the Discourses and a short handbook. Through them, you can hear him in class. In one passage, he imagines a tyrant threatening him. You'll chain me? You can chain my leg. But my will, not even Zeus himself can take that. In another, he tells how a thief stole the iron lamp from his little shrine at home. His response: next time I'll buy a clay one. And then the twist: the thief lost more than I did. He paid for a lamp by becoming a thief. The Greek word he kept coming back to was prohairesis, usually translated will, or choice: your power to decide how you'll meet what happens. Epictetus had been owned, lamed, freed, exiled. Everything outside kept being taken. And that's the point of the story. The school at Nicopolis was real, with benches and walls. But the school he actually taught was one you carry inside. No emperor can banish it.
screen: `EXILED BY DOMITIAN.` · `A SCHOOL AT NICOPOLIS.` · `YOU CAN CHAIN MY LEG.` · `THE THIEF LOST MORE.` · then, large: `THE SCHOOL IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then ask yourself: what's one thing no one can take from me? Not an object. Something inside. The way you treat people. Your sense of humor. A memory. What you choose to pay attention to. Let an answer come, and rest with it. If you have paper nearby, after the bell, write it down in one line. The bell holds the time.
prohairesis, usually translated will, or choice: your power to decide how you'll meet what happens. Freed, then exiled, and still teaching: a school at Nicopolis, and one you carry inside.
Your line: the school is inside. Today, write down the one thing no one can take, and put it somewhere you'll see it. Day twenty-four.

howItsDone: Modern Stoics often keep a short written list of what is truly in their power, their own choices and responses, and read the Discourses and Handbook of Epictetus as a daily guide.

fork.setup: you're Epictetus, and a thief has stolen the iron lamp from your home. what do you do?
options: buy a cheaper clay lamp, and decide the thief lost more.
fork.reveal: a clay lamp next time. and the thief? he paid for a lamp by becoming a thief.

original.note: Greek, prohairesis: will, choice, the power to decide how you meet what happens. Epictetus's central word.

trapdoor: what you thought: a slave who got lucky and was freed.
what it means: a man who kept losing everything outside, and taught a school no one could take.

what a scholar hears: Aulus Gellius 15.11 has Epictetus leave Rome for Nicopolis when Domitian expelled the philosophers; the year is disputed. Arrian's Discourses 1.1 and 1.18 give the chained leg and the stolen lamp.

sources.ref: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 15.11 (Domitian's expulsion of the philosophers)

notes: Date of Domitian's expulsion: c. 89 CE or 93–95 CE; the index says 'around 93 CE' and the script hedges.
Epictetus studied under Musonius Rufus while still enslaved (Discourses 1.7.32, 1.9.29); confirm.
The lamp story: iron lamp stolen, he plans an earthenware one (Discourses 1.18.15); 'the thief lost more' paraphrases the point (he became a thief for a lamp; see also 1.29.21). Confirm.
Discourses 1.1.23: 'my leg you will fetter, but my will not even Zeus can overpower' paraphrased, not quoted.
Date of his manumission is unknown; script says so.
